title: Arrays & hashing
summary: Walk the list once and keep what you have seen in a hash map or set, so each lookup is instant instead of another loop.
idea: Trade memory for time: remember each item in a map as you pass it, then answer questions about earlier items in O(1).

signals.see: The question asks if two items match, pair up or repeat.
signals.think: Store each item in a set or map. Before storing, ask: have I already seen what would complete the answer?

signals.see: A brute force needs two nested loops over the same list.
signals.think: The inner loop is a search. Replace it with a map lookup to go from O(n²) to O(n).

signals.see: Items must be grouped or counted by some key.
signals.think: Build a map from key to a count or a list. Pick a key that is the same for items that belong together.

signals.see: Order of the input does not matter for the answer.
signals.think: A set or map can stand in for sorting. Membership checks are O(1).

phrasings: Given a list of order totals, return the positions of two orders that together spend exactly a gift card's value.
A help desk logs ticket ids. Report the first ticket id that was opened twice.
Group product names that are spelled with the same letters.

picture.title: Remember instead of re-scanning
picture.alt: On the left, every item starts a fresh scan of the whole list, giving n times n checks. On the right, each item is looked up in a map, then added to it, giving one pass.
picture.caption: The map answers “have I seen what I need?” in one step, so the inner loop disappears.

code.py:
def pair_with_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}  #@init
    for i in range(len(nums)):  #@loop
        need = target - nums[i]  #@need
        if need in seen: return [seen[need], i]  #@found
        seen[nums[i]] = i  #@store
    return []  #@none

visualiser.inputHelp: Up to 12 whole numbers between -99 and 99, separated by commas. The target is one whole number.

oneLiner: for x in items: if need(x) in seen: answer; seen[x] = info

hints: A set answers “have I seen this code?” in one step.
Check the set before you add the code. If you add first, every code looks like a repeat.

complexity.why: Each item is looked up and stored once, and a hash lookup takes O(1) on average. In the worst case the map holds every item.

mistakes: Storing the item before checking for it, so it matches itself.
Using a list instead of a set or map, which makes each lookup O(n) again.
Forgetting duplicates: decide whether the map should keep the first index, the last index or a count.
Using a mutable key, such as a list in Python. Turn it into a tuple or a string first.
Not handling the empty list or a list with one item.

quiz.question: Why does a hash map turn a pair search from O(n²) into O(n)?
choices: It replaces the inner search loop with an O(1) average lookup
It skips half of the items
quiz.explain: The brute force looks for a partner with a second loop. The map remembers earlier items, so finding a partner is one lookup.

quiz.question: In a one-pass pair search, why check the map before adding the current item?
choices: So an item cannot pair with itself
quiz.explain: If you add first, an item whose partner is itself (like 5 for target 10) would match its own entry.

quiz.question: You need to group words that use the same letters. What makes a good map key?
choices: The word's letters in sorted order
quiz.explain: Words with the same letters sort to the same string, so they land under the same key. Length or first letter mixes groups.

interviewTip: Say the brute force first (“two loops, O(n²)”), then say what the inner loop is looking for. Naming that as a map lookup is the whole pattern, and it shows the interviewer how you got there.
